feedback: If a learner calls the knowledge 'just stories' or 'luck', point to the concrete examples, the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark, where modern chemists studied the same plants and confirmed the effect.
If a learner speaks in the past tense ('they used to know'), correct gently to present tense: these are living communities who hold and use this knowledge today.

Reinforce correct answers by naming the two-way link: for these documented plants (the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark) the forest people knew the use first and modern chemists later studied and confirmed it, and more broadly science continues to learn from this knowledge.
activities.intendedInsight: Indigenous ecological knowledge is detailed, empirical expertise — and for several documented plants, modern science later studied and confirmed the same effect — not folklore or stories.
learnerActions: Examine a scene showing several rainforest plants, each paired with a traditional use: a slender vine used to stun fish for easy catching, a bark used to ease fever, a fruit tree providing both food and building wood.

For each plant, state its traditional use in your own words. For the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark, read the added note that chemists later studied the very same plant or a substance from it (the vine's fish-stunning substance and the bark's fever medicine); the fruit tree simply shows food and building wood.
Explain aloud why 'the people of the forest knew this first' shows real expertise rather than luck or guesswork.
Give at least two examples of indigenous forest knowledge from memory.
activities.title: Forest pharmacy: plants and their tested uses

feedback: If a learner says 'any cutting of trees destroys the forest', contrast scale and permanence: a small plot left to regrow for long enough is a sustainable cycle, unlike large permanent clearing for cattle ranches or soy and palm-oil plantations.
If a learner conflates small rotational plots with large-scale slash-and-burn, separate the two explicitly: the problem is clearing huge areas permanently, not farming a small plot and moving on.
Confirm full answers that name all three ideas: small plot, left to regrow, soil restores.
activities.intendedInsight: Small-scale, rotational clearing left to regrow for long enough is a sustainable cycle; it is large scale, permanence, or rest periods too short for recovery — not any tree-cutting at all — that destroy rainforest.
learnerActions: Follow a small clearing through its full cycle: a small plot is opened, cropped for a few years, then left to rest while the forest slowly closes back over it.

Beside it, observe a permanently cleared strip, shown in this illustration as bare and cracked, that never regrows into forest and becomes degraded because the nutrient-poor soil is used up and never rested.
Explain in your own words what shifting cultivation is and why it harms the forest less than permanent clearing (the plot is small, is left to regrow, and the soil restores).
Answer the probe: if a shifting-cultivation patch were never left to regrow, would it still be sustainable? Explain why not.
activities.title: The shifting-cultivation cycle vs permanent clearance

feedback: If the learner frames the expert as 'primitive' or from 'long ago', redirect: these are living experts with sophisticated, tested knowledge.
If the learner suggests science should 'correct' the knowledge, reframe as two-way: traditional knowledge and science complement each other toward a shared goal.
Affirm follow-up questions that show genuine curiosity and respectful listening.
activities.intendedInsight: Indigenous peoples are contemporary experts; a learner can follow curiosity to understand their expertise and how it complements modern science.
learnerActions: Take the role of a respectful learner asking a knowledge-holder questions such as 'How do you farm without exhausting the soil?' and 'Which plant would you use for a fever?'
Listen to the expert's spoken answers and ask a follow-up question driven by your own curiosity.
Afterwards, retell two things the expert taught you, using present tense.
Describe how this knowledge and modern science could work together to protect the forest.

Optionally, look at a map of forest peoples and the biodiverse territories they steward, and at an image showing traditional knowledge and lab science converging on a shared goal, to see that these are contemporary communities whose expertise works alongside science today.
activities.title: Learning from the expert: a respectful apprentice dialogue
